facts.summary: Maryland requires overtime at 1.5x the regular rate only after 40 hours in a 7-day week, with no daily overtime rule, mirroring federal FLSA.
facts.citation: Md. Code, Labor & Employment Art., Title 3, Subtitle 4 (§ 3-415)
facts.sourceAgency: Maryland Department of Labor, Division of Labor and Industry (Employment Standards Service)
facts.notes: Some occupations differ (e.g., certain agricultural workers get OT after 60 hrs/week). No higher salary floor than federal; state defers to federal EAP exemptions.

facts.summary: Maryland's statewide minimum wage is $15.00 per hour for all employers under the Fair Wage Act; some counties (e.g., Montgomery County) set a higher local minimum wage that applies instead.
facts.sourceAgency: Maryland Department of Labor, Division of Labor and Industry (Employment Standards Service)
facts.notes: Higher local rates apply: Montgomery County (up to $18.00 for 51+ employees as of 7/1/2026), Howard County ($16.00), Prince George's County ($15.30 as of 1/1/2026). Employers may pay 85% of state rate to workers under 18. Verify current statewide figure annually.

facts.summary: Maryland prohibits employment discrimination on several bases beyond the federal set, including marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, military status, and race-associated traits such as hairstyle (CROWN Act).
facts.notes: Full Maryland list also includes the federal bases (race, color, religion, ancestry/national origin, sex, age, disability, genetic information). Listed here are additions/expansions beyond the federal Title VII/ADA/ADEA set.

facts.value: 15+ employees for discrimination; 1+ employee for harassment
facts.summary: Maryland's general discrimination protections apply to employers with 15 or more employees (same as federal), but harassment claims may be brought against employers with just one or more employees.
facts.notes: The lowered 1-employee threshold for harassment (added by 2019 amendments) is the key state addition beyond the federal 15-employee floor.

facts.value: mandatory for employees and applicants absent undue hardship
facts.summary: Maryland's Fair Employment Practices Act makes it unlawful for a covered employer to fail or refuse to make reasonable accommodation for the known disability of an otherwise-qualified employee or job applicant.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text (fetched from mgaleg.maryland.gov): 20-606(a)(4) already covers both an 'employee' and 'an applicant for employment.' The undue-hardship exception and the requirement that employers consider reassignment to other available positions (not just the employee's current job) are set out in implementing COMAR 14.03.02 regulations and Fourth Circuit case law, not independently verified against primary regulatory text this session. Applies at the 15+-employee coverage threshold (see discrimination.coverage, above).

facts.summary: A discrimination or retaliation complaint must be filed with MCCR within 300 days of the alleged act, while harassment complaints have a 2-year filing window.
facts.notes: The 2-year harassment filing period exceeds the federal EEOC 300-day maximum and is a state-specific extension.

facts.value: 3 years (court lawsuit); 2 years (administrative claim with ESS)
facts.summary: Unpaid-wage lawsuits under Maryland law have a 3-year statute of limitations, but an administrative wage claim filed with the Department of Labor's Employment Standards Service must be received within 2 years of the wages becoming due.
facts.citation: Md. Code, Labor & Employment Art., §§ 3-427, 3-507.2 (general 3-yr limitations under Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-101)
facts.sourceAgency: Maryland Department of Labor, Division of Labor and Industry (Employment Standards Service)
facts.notes: Courts may award up to 3x wages plus attorney's fees for withholding not based on a bona fide dispute. Verify exact statutory cross-references.

facts.value: MOSH safety/health whistleblower protection; complaint within 30 days
facts.summary: Maryland prohibits employers from discharging or discriminating against employees for exercising occupational safety and health rights, with complaints filed to the MOSH Commissioner within 30 days of the alleged retaliation.
facts.sourceAgency: Maryland Department of Labor, Maryland Occupational Safety and Health (MOSH)
facts.notes: This covers safety/health retaliation. Maryland also has separate whistleblower statutes for state employees and health care workers; verify statute cross-reference for § 5-604.

facts.value: due by next regular payday after termination
facts.summary: Maryland requires an employer to pay all wages due to a separated employee on or before the regular payday on which the wages would have been paid had employment continued.
facts.sourceAgency: Maryland Department of Labor, Division of Labor and Industry (Employment Standards Service)
facts.notes: Accrued unused vacation must be paid out unless the employer had a written forfeiture policy communicated at hire. Severance is not required unless promised by contract or policy.
